A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VideoLLaMB. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and relocation of material.

before.justification: v1 reports original VideoQA, EgoPlan, NIAVH, computational-efficiency and ablation results, including parameter experiments in Appendix A.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds VideoMME evaluation, latency breakdowns and compression-strategy comparisons.

M1.justification: The stated streaming SceneTiling score changes from (left similarity + s_i)/2 in v1 Section 3.4 to (left similarity - c_i)/2 in v2 Section 3.5. This revises the documented boundary-detection procedure; implementation changes are not established. The recurrent bridge, retrieval mechanism and offline segmentation procedure are retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds VideoMME evaluation on videos ranging from 11 seconds to one hour, substantially extending natural-video QA duration coverage beyond the earlier EgoSchema, NExTQA and MVBench evaluations. Existing training collections, planning, streaming-caption and NIAVH coverage are retained.

E2.justification: The EgoPlan table drops Qwen-VL-Chat, LLaVA-1.5, SEED-LLaMA, InternLM-Xcomposer, VideoChatGPT and Valley. The NIAVH heatmap comparison drops PLLaVA and LLaVA-NeXT-Video-DPO, although their aggregate scores remain. Conversely, Figure 2 adds LLaVA-NeXT-Video to length extrapolation, and Appendix B adds MovieChat-derived token compression to the controlled EgoSchema comparison.

E3.justification: New protocols include comparisons holding the LLM, training data and compression rate fixed in Appendix B, feature-processing versus generation timing at 30, 300 and 3000 seconds, and a k=8 ablation. VideoMME introduces duration-group reporting and a compression column. Retained experiments largely preserve their stated evaluation protocols.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled compression-strategy analysis, a k=8 sensitivity result and latency decomposition by video duration. The length-extrapolation comparison is extended, while the separate VideoLLaMB-R memory-cost series disappears. Existing component ablations, parameter analysis and qualitative examples are otherwise retained, with the examples moved to Appendix D.

E5.justification: Both versions report point accuracies and average scores without reported seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests. v2 introduces no new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: New results include VideoMME overall scores of 39.59 and 41.41 for the two training-data variants, k=8 accuracy of 52.8, compression comparisons and latency breakdowns. Existing plots also change: Figure 2's dynamic-segment accuracy at 64 frames rises from approximately 53.6 to 53.8, and GPU-memory values are revised. Several comparator results disappear, while matched entries in Tables 1–3 remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 2.2 changes the stated complexity of traditional recurrent-memory Transformers from O(LK) to O(L^2/K). The streaming depth-score definition also changes non-equivalently. The proposed bridge's complexity expressions remain unchanged, and no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract revises the claimed VideoQA advantage from 5.5 points across three benchmarks to 4.2 points across four, with VideoMME added to the introduction's coverage claim. The central memory-bridge, NIAVH, training-free streaming-captioning and 2.06-point planning claims are retained.

C2.justification: v2 removes the qualification that certain image-language models outperform VideoLLaMB on EgoPlan and the explanation involving brief action sequences and curated frame-action pairs. Limitations concerning training-length mismatch, forgetting and hallucinations remain. The new compression comparison supplies additional support for the existing memory-retention interpretation.

D1.justification: v2 defines the parenthesized training-frame counts in Table 1 and newly states a default evaluation configuration in Section 3.1. It removes v1's explicit instruction that NIAVH feeds memory tokens into the LLM. The appendix hyperparameters, hardware, initialization and code link are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including VideoMME, Video-XL, Loogle, OmniMMI and TokenSwift, and removes references associated with omitted planning baselines. It expands discussion of comparison fairness while retaining the related-work taxonomy and NIAVH versus MM-NIAH positioning. Publication updates to existing references do not constitute new work.

P1.justification: The abstract, opening motivation, contribution list and conclusion are substantially rewritten. MVBench and ablations receive separate subsections, qualitative material is regrouped in Appendix D, and the supplementary structure is reorganized. The title, authorship and terminology also change.

P2.justification: The document is redesigned from one column to two, with extensive repositioning and resizing. v2 adds VideoMME, latency and compression tables, reduces the planning table and NIAVH panel grid, and redraws the extrapolation and memory plots with changed legends and axes. Existing qualitative figures move to the appendix.

improvement.justification: VideoMME, the controlled compression comparison and latency decomposition provide useful additional evidence for long-video understanding, memory retention and efficiency. These modestly strengthen the empirical case. The benefit is partly offset by reduced EgoPlan and NIAVH comparison coverage and removal of the EgoPlan limitation, so the overall improvement is limited.
